If Cadm4, MAG, and Cntn1b function redundantly to stabilize axon–oligodendrocyte adhesion during CNS myelination, then simultaneous knockout of cadm4, mag, and cntn1b in zebrafish will cause more severe defects in myelinated axon density, myelin sheath formation and stability, compaction, and axon caliber than loss of cadm4 and mag alone or single knockouts, because these molecules share overlapping roles in maintaining glial–axonal interactions.

If Cadm4 functions redundantly with MAG and contactin1b to mediate oligodendrocyte–axon adhesion and myelin sheath stabilization, then cadm4−/−mag−/− and cadm4−/−cntn1b−/−mag−/− zebrafish will show decreased myelinated area, increased myelin sheath retraction/stubs and ectopic cell body ensheathment, and altered axon diameter distributions compared with wild type, because simultaneous loss of these molecules disrupts myelin recognition, wrapping, and compaction.

If cadm4, mag, and cntn1b encode functionally redundant axon–oligodendrocyte adhesion molecules required for CNS myelin sheath formation and stability, then their combinatorial loss in zebrafish will cause dose-dependent reductions in myelinated area, myelin sheath number and length, sheath stabilization, and myelin ultrastructural integrity because deletion of these adhesion molecules disrupts axon–glial interactions essential for myelin assembly and maintenance.

If Cadm4, MAG, and CNTN1b are deleted together in zebrafish, then myelin sheath initiation, stabilization, and maintenance will be more severely disrupted than in single or double knockouts because these proteins redundantly mediate axon–oligodendrocyte adhesion required for normal myelination.
